definition: A tendency for evaluators to favor responses based on their order or position when comparing multiple candidates, rather than purely on content quality.
details: Position bias is a known issue in pairwise comparison evaluations (including LLM-as-a-judge setups), where simply swapping the order of two candidate responses can change which one is judged as better, motivating techniques like order randomization.

explainer.lead: Position bias is evaluators favouring a response because of its order in a comparison rather than its content. It matters because pairwise evaluations, including LLM-as-a-judge setups, can flip verdicts when candidates are swapped.

tiers.eli5: Like a taste test where the first sample always seems better, even when the two cups hold the same drink.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers mitigate it by randomising or swapping response order across comparisons; a pitfall is assuming a judge is order-invariant without testing the swap.
tiers.paperLevel: Defined as a tendency in pairwise comparison evaluation to favour responses by their order or position rather than content quality; swapping order can change the judged winner.

explainer.example: A judge prefers response A over B, but when the two are presented in the reverse order it prefers B, revealing position bias.
